title: 15 Ways to Find Data Fast (And When Each Fails)
subtitle: Pick the right database index or pay for it later
intro: A well-designed index can speed up queries by orders of magnitude, while the wrong index can slow everything down. With 15 options in 2026, how do you choose?
takeaway: An index trades write speed and space for read speed, so match the index shape to your query shape.

sections.heading: Analogy: indexes are like book helpers
sections.body:
Imagine data is a giant library with no help. Finding one page would mean checking every book.

An index is like a helper list at the front: a B-Tree is the sorted table of contents for range queries, a Hash Index is the exact-page finder for equality lookups like key 123, and an Inverted Index is the word-to-page list behind search.

Pick the helper that matches how you search, and you skip the full scan.

But every helper costs paper and upkeep, which is why choice matters next.

sections.heading: Why does this exist? Speed you don't pay for twice
sections.body:
Databases need different indexes because queries are different shapes.

- B-Tree and B+ Tree: balanced, disk-friendly range scans, used in MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, InnoDB.
- Hash Index: lightning-fast equality in key-value and in-memory stores.
- LSM Tree: high write throughput via sequential writes, used in Cassandra, RocksDB, Bigtable.
- Inverted Index: backbone of Elasticsearch and Lucene for full-text search.

That speed has a price, and the next part shows the bill.

sections.heading: What can go wrong? The wrong shortcut hurts
sections.body:
Every index trades space and write speed for read speed.

A Hash Index cannot do range queries. A B-Tree slows writes that an LSM Tree handles well. A Bitmap Index works for low-cardinality filters in OLAP, not high-cardinality data.

Add too many indexes and inserts crawl while storage bloats.

So ask first: is my query equality, range, text search, or heavy write?

steps.narration: Start with a query that would otherwise scan everything.
Use B-Tree for sorted range queries.
Use Hash for exact equality lookups.
Use LSM when writes must stay fast.

quiz.q: Why use a B+ Tree instead of a Hash Index?
options: B+ Tree is faster for equality only
B+ Tree handles range scans with linked leaves, Hash does not
B+ Tree is only for text search
quiz.why: From saves: B+ Tree optimized for range scans, Hash is for lightning-fast equality lookups only.

quiz.q: What fails first if write traffic grows 100x with many B-Tree indexes?
options: Writes slow down due to index maintenance on every insert
quiz.why: Wrong indexes slow everything down; each extra B-Tree must be updated on writes, while LSM is designed for high write throughput.

quiz.q: Which index is the backbone of Elasticsearch for keyword matching?
quiz.why: Saves list Inverted Index as backbone of Elasticsearch, Lucene for full-text search.
